absaetze.t: EuroQuestions : Saison 2026, Épisode 20
Date / Lieu : Le 25 novembre 2026, de 16:30 à 17:30, en ligne (sur inscription)
Titre :
Briefing Delors : à l’approche du Conseil Européen, 26-27 novembre 2026
Contexte :

L’Institut Jacques Delors a lancé un nouveau rendez-vous au sein des EuroQuestions: Briefing Delors : à l’approche du Conseil Européen. Cette session réunira quatre experts de l’Institut Jacques Delors pour apporter les clés de compréhension du contexte dans lequel se tient ce Conseil européen extraordinaire : priorités à l’ordre du jour, positions des États membres, état des négociations et principaux enjeux.

À la suite du Sommet de la Communauté politique européenne et de la réunion informelle des chefs d’État ou de gouvernement de l’UE, et à l’approche du Sommet UE-Balkans occidentaux du 25 novembre et du Conseil européen extraordinaire des 26 et 27 novembre, cette séquence permettra de revenir sur les grandes priorités politiques européennes :

Le prochain cadre financier pluriannuel (2028-2034) devrait occuper une place centrale lors du Conseil européen extraordinaire. Alors que les négociations s’intensifient, Eulalia Rubio, chercheuse senior en affaires économiques européennes, fera le point sur leur état d’avancement, les conclusions du dernier Conseil européen et les objectifs du président António Costa.

L’Ukraine et la sécurité européenne resteront au cœur des préoccupations, dans un contexte marqué par les négociations russo-américaines et les discussions sur les garanties de sécurité et de soutien à l’Ukraine. Sylvie Matelly, conseillère en Économie de la Défense, reviendra sur les derniers développements diplomatiques, les positions des États européens et les perspectives pour la sécurité du continent.

L’élargissement de l’Union européenne connaîtra également une séquence politique importante, entre la publication du rapport annuel sur l’élargissement de la Commission, le Forum sur l’élargissement et le Sommet UE-Balkans occidentaux. Benjamin Couteau, chercheur au Centre Grande Europe, présentera les principaux enseignements de ces rendez-vous et les perspectives d’avancement des négociations, notamment avec le Monténégro et l’Albanie.

Enfin, l’intelligence artificielle s’est imposée dans les discussions européennes, notamment lors de la récente retraite informelle des dirigeants. Arnault Barichella, chercheur associé sur le numérique, le cyber et l’IA, reviendra sur les raisons de cette réunion, les principaux enjeux abordés et les enseignements à tirer pour la stratégie européenne en matière d’IA.

En une heure, le Briefing Delors entend ainsi donner les principales cartes en main pour comprendre cette séquence européenne : son contexte politique, les rapports de force entre États membres, l’état des négociations et les dossiers susceptibles de structurer les prochains mois.
Questions à approfondir :
Quels éléments du contexte (géo)politique actuels sont susceptibles de peser sur ce Conseil européen ?
Sur chacun des sujets à l’ordre du jour, quels sont les principaux points de désaccord et entre quels États membres ?
Quelle est la position de la France sur ces différents sujets et comment se situe-t-elle par rapport aux autres États membres ?
Présentation intervenant.e.s :

Eulalia Rubio, chercheuse senior à l’Institut Jacques Delors, est spécialiste du budget de l’Union européenne, de la politique budgétaire et des investissements publics européens. Elle a notamment travaillé sur le plan de relance post-Covid, le rôle de la Banque européenne d’investissement et le financement de la transition écologique et industrielle.

Sylvie Matelly, conseillère à l’Institut Jacques Delors qu’elle a dirigé d’octobre 2023 à août 2026, est économiste et professeure associée au Centre for Global Risks de SKEMA Business School. Auparavant directrice adjointe de l’IRIS (2016-2023), elle est spécialiste des questions de géopolitique et d’économie de la défense, notamment des industries de défense, du contrôle des exportations et de la corruption. Docteure en économie internationale, elle est également l’auteure de plusieurs ouvrages, dont Géopolitique de l’économie (2026).

Benjamin Couteau est chercheur au Centre Grande Europe de l’Institut Jacques Delors depuis 2022, spécialisé dans l’élargissement de l’UE, les Balkans occidentaux, la Turquie et les influences concurrentes dans la région. Ancien responsable de plusieurs groupes de travail de l’Institut et de l’Académie Notre Europe, il est diplômé en droit européen et international de l’Université de Bordeaux et en droits de l’Homme et droit de l’UE de l’Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne.

Arnault Barichella est chercheur associé à l’Institut Jacques Delors depuis septembre 2022, où il travaille sur les enjeux de cybersécurité, des technologies numériques et de l’intelligence artificielle. Ses recherches portent notamment sur la régulation européenne de l’IA, la protection des données et les liens entre cybersécurité et conflits armés. Il est actuellement chercheur postdoctoral en sciences sociales à l’Université Paris-Saclay et titulaire d’un doctorat en science politique de Sciences Po Paris. Il est également rédacteur en chef du Palgrave Handbook of Cybersecurity, Technologies and Energy Transitions.
Les EuroQuestions, c’est quoi ?

Les EuroQuestions sont des sessions organisées deux à trois fois par mois sous la forme d’échanges en ligne de 30 minutes réunissant un modérateur (Mme Christine Verger ou M. William Malaterre) et un intervenant invité autour d’une question européenne d’actualité. L’intervenant dispose généralement d’un temps de présentation d’environ 15 à 20 minutes, suivi d’un échange de 10 à 15 minutes avec le modérateur.

items.titel: Mit 65 Jahren: Duran-Duran-Gitarrist Andy Taylor gestorben
items.anriss: Andy Taylor, der ursprüngliche Gitarrist der englischen New-Wave-Band Duran Duran, ist gestorben. Mit seinen von Rock und Funk inspirierten Gitarrenriffs prägte Taylor den Sound der Band.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Andy Taylor, der ursprüngliche Gitarrist der englischen New-Wave-Band Duran Duran, ist gestorben. Mit seinen von Rock und Funk inspirierten Gitarrenriffs prägte Taylor den Sound der Band.

Andy Taylor, der ehemalige Gitarrist der britischen Gruppe Duran Duran, ist tot. Er sei am Montag "nach einem langen und mutigen Kampf gegen Prostatakrebs" friedlich zu Hause im Kreis seiner Familie gestorben, hieß es in einer am Mittwochabend veröffentlichten Erklärung seiner Familie und der aus Birmingham stammenden Band. Er wurde 65 Jahre alt.

Taylor wurde am 16. Februar 1961 nahe Newcastle im Nordosten Englands geboren und begann im Alter von elf Jahren, Gitarre zu spielen. Auf eine Anzeige in einer Musikzeitschrift hin schloss er sich im April 1980 der zwei Jahre zuvor in Birmingham gegründeten Band an.
Duran Duran am 12. Oktober 2004 im The Sony Club in New York. Von links: Roger Taylor, Nick Rhodes, Andy Taylor, Simon Le Bon und John Taylor.
Wichtiger Teil von Duran Duran

Mit seinen von Rock und Funk inspirierten Gitarrenriffs prägte Taylor den unverwechselbaren Sound von Duran Duran, der Elemente des Punkrock mit Tanzmusik verband. Er wirkte an den ersten drei Alben der Band mit, die zwischen 1981 und 1983 erschienen.

Duran Duran war in den 80er Jahren eine der erfolgreichsten Popbands und zählte zu den Initiatoren einer Poprock-Richtung namens New Romantic. Die Band um Sänger Simon Le Bon schrieb Popklassiker wie "Girls On Film", "The Wild Boys", "Hungry Like the Wolf", "The Reflex" oder "A View to a Kill".
Lange Krebserkrankung

Bei der Einführungszeremonie der Band in die "Rock & Roll Hall of Fame" vor gut vier Jahren hatte Taylor seine Krankheit verkündet. In einem bei der Veranstaltung in Los Angeles vorgelesenen Brief schrieb er, der Krebs sei unheilbar. Duran Duran wurde damals in die Ruhmeshalle in Cleveland im US-Bundesstaat Ohio aufgenommen.

2006 hatte Taylor die Band im Streit während einer US-Tournee verlassen. Zwischen ihm und den anderen vier Bandmitgliedern sei es zu einer "unüberbrückbaren Kluft" gekommen, hieß es damals. Dies habe eine weitere Zusammenarbeit unmöglich gemacht.

items.titel: Houthis target Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports as strikes escalate
items.anriss: Explosion reported in Sanaa after Saudi air defenses intercept ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh.

absaetze.t: Explosion reported in Sanaa after Saudi air defenses intercept ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh.
Yemen’s Houthi group has struck the port of Jizan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast as fighting intensifies near the Yemeni city of Taiz.

A Saudi-led military coalition said a Houthi attack on Jizan caused only minor damage and no civilian casualties on Wednesday, adding that “efforts are underway to determine the type of projectile” used.
The spokesman for the coalition, Turki al-Maliki, later said in a statement on X that its forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone over Jeddah’s port in Saudi Arabia.
No civilian injuries were reported from falling debris following the interception, he added.
After the coalition’s statement, an explosion was heard in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, according to Al Jazeera’s Nabil al-Yousfi.
The Saudi-led coalition then said its air defences intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh.
The attempted strike on the capital follows a Houthi drone attack on a skyscraper in Riyadh’s financial district on Tuesday, injuring at least 11 people.

The latest incidents mark a further escalation between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia, including strikes from both sides targeting airports, energy facilities and other civilian and economic infrastructure.
The strikes on Saudi Arabian ports come after the Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported new Saudi attacks on the port of Hodeidah in Yemen.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Houthis threatened to attack Saudi ports if Hodeidah came under attack.

“The port of Hodeidah handles 90 percent of imported goods into Yemen. If it is closed, it could bring the humanitarian situation to the brink of collapse”, said Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.
“Some of Saudi Arabia’s recent attacks at the Port of Hodeidah have targeted storage tanks and cranes used to load and unload shipments”, Mawry said.
Fighting in Yemen

Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have been battling the Houthis on several fronts, with the army’s spokesman saying 654 strikes have been carried out against the group on Wednesday.
Yemen’s western front has witnessed the heaviest concentration of recent strikes, according to Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz.
Government forces have said air strikes targeted Houthi positions west of Taiz.
“These strikes are part of an intense and sustained wave of air raids that have continued for approximately 72 hours”, Ali said.

“Particular attention is focused on the most significant mountain range overlooking central Taiz: Jabal Saber and its highest peak, Jabal al-Arus. The government says the Houthis want to seize this strategic peak”, she added.
The Houthis said there have been 105 air strikes and missile attacks by the Saudi-led coalition targeting civilian sites in Sanaa and 10 governorates on Wednesday.

items.titel: Malen and Roma deny injury-hit PSG in Champions League draw
items.anriss: Champions League holders Paris Saint-Germain held to 2-2 draw by Roma as injury-ravaged squad struggle.

absaetze.t: Champions League holders Paris Saint-Germain held to 2-2 draw by Roma as injury-ravaged squad struggle.

Donyell Malen’s penalty gave Roma a 2-2 draw away to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday, as the injury-hit reigning champions saw their perfect record in this season’s competition come to an end.

Malen stroked in from the spot in the 78th minute on a bitterly cold and wet night at the Parc des Princes, giving Roma a welcome point after their collapse from two goals up to lose 3-2 at Manchester United last time out.
Roma had earlier taken the lead through Mario Hermoso, only for Illia Zabarnyi to equalise before substitute Ousmane Dembele put PSG briefly in front with a penalty of his own.
The result ends PSG’s perfect record in this season’s league phase, and halts a run of 12 consecutive wins in all competitions for Luis Enrique’s team.
They fall two points behind Real Madrid, who are now clear at the top of the standings as the only side still with a 100 percent record after five matches.

It is only a minor setback for PSG in their quest to finish in the top eight of the 36-team table, and therefore qualify directly for the last 16 without having to go through the playoff round like in the last two campaigns.

But the Parisians could have done with the boost of a victory as they come to terms with the loss of the outstanding Desire Doue, who may not play again this season after rupturing the ACL in his right knee last weekend.

Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, another of their outstanding attacking players, recently succumbed to the same injury, while Dembele has been struggling for fitness, too, and PSG’s prospects of winning a third straight Champions League title are undoubtedly diminished as a result.

Dembele’s presence on the bench at kickoff meant that none of PSG’s five top scorers from last season was in their line-up here, with the others either injured or having departed in the case of Bradley Barcola and Goncalo Ramos.

Meanwhile, Roma coach Gian Piero Gasperini raised eyebrows by leaving Malen out of his starting XI. The Dutchman is running at an average of more than a goal a game this season and netted four against Parma last weekend.
However, Roma have been in prolific form in general, netting 26 goals in their last seven matches before arriving in the French capital.
They went ahead inside five minutes here as Matias Soule cut the ball back from the byline and Spanish defender Hermoso was on hand to convert.

Roma had blown even more promising leads already this season, though, losing 4-3 at home to Real Madrid after leading 3-1 with eight minutes left, and then going down 3-2 at Old Trafford despite being 2-0 ahead at half-time.
Ukrainian defender Zabarnyi levelled just after the half-hour mark as he found space at the near post to head in Senny Mayulu’s corner.
Evan Ndicka headed just off-target for Roma late in the first half, and Niccolo Pisilli forced a good stop from Matvei Safonov early in the second half.
Joao Neves then headed agonisingly wide for PSG as he arrived unmarked in the area to meet a Nuno Mendes cross, before Dembele was introduced for the hosts in place of the ineffective Ferran Torres.
Moments after that, PSG won a penalty when Achraf Hakimi stormed into the Roma box only to be pulled down by Wesley.
The French side had missed four penalties in the Champions League since the start of last season, but Dembele did score in the final against Arsenal in May.
He kept a cool head to convert his fifth goal of the campaign, but PSG could not make it five straight Champions League wins this season.
Malen entered the fray for Roma midway through the second half and looked on as Dembele was denied a brilliant solo goal by a Mile Svilar save.
Roma then won a penalty following a VAR check after Vitinha blocked a Soule shot with a raised hand in the box.
Up stepped Malen to score his 17th goal of a prolific campaign, boosting Roma’s hopes of reaching the knockout phase.

items.titel: US-Armee sprengt vier Tonnen giftigen Sprengstoff
items.anriss: Von dem gelagerten Sprengstoff ging laut der US-Armee eine Gefahr aus. Deshalb war die Sprengung nötig.

absaetze.t: Die US-Armee hat im Bundesstaat Iowa tonnenweise giftigen Sprengstoff kontrolliert zur Explosion gebracht.
Laut dem Militär war die Sprengung auf dem Gelände einer Munitionsfabrik notwendig, weil die Gefahr einer unkontrollierten Explosion bestand.
Umweltgruppen äusserten die Sorge, giftiger Bleistaub könne sich über der Gegend ausbreiten.

Der Sprengstoff habe begonnen, sich zu zersetzen und Kristalle zu bilden, teilte die US-Armee mit. Laut der US-Umweltbehörde EPA bestand durch den degradierten Zustand des Bleiazids eine «unmittelbare und erhebliche Bedrohung für die menschliche Gesundheit und die Umwelt».

Der Sprengung waren tagelange Diskussionen vorausgegangen. Die Armee kündigte an, ein kleiner Teil der Wolke werde aus feinem Bleioxidstaub bestehen. Umweltgruppen etwa hatten die Sorge geäussert, giftiger Bleistaub könne sich über Teile des ländlichen Iowa und des nordöstlichen Missouri ausbreiten. Bleiazid ist ein hochexplosiver Initialsprengstoff, der aufgrund seines Bleigehalts auch umwelt- und gesundheitsschädlich ist. Luftmessungen der EPA zeigten nach der Explosion zunächst keinen Anstieg der Bleibelastung in der Luft. Es wird aber weiter getestet.

Die Einwohner des Ortes Middletown waren zur Evakuierung aufgerufen. Bewohnern der Umgebung wurde geraten, in ihren Häusern zu bleiben, Fenster und Türen zu schliessen sowie Futter und Wasser für Nutztiere und Nutzpflanzen abzudecken. Besondere Vorsicht wurde Schwangeren, Säuglingen und Kindern unter sechs Jahren geraten. Nach der Entwarnung sollten Anwohner Terrassen, Fensterbänke und Spielgeräte im Freien abwischen, um abgelagerten Staub sicher zu entfernen.

Man habe die Sprengung eigentlich vermeiden wollen, hiess es von der Armee, aber keine praktikable Alternative finden können. Die knapp 70 Fässer mit 4.4 Tonnen Bleiazid hatten wegen der Explosionsgefahr nicht mehr bewegt werden können.

items.titel: Carla Babb Named Head of Content for Military Times and Defense News
items.anriss: Carla Babb is joining Military Times and Defense News as our new Head of Content. In nearly two decades covering national security and international affairs, Babb has earned a reputation for fearless, fact-driven journalism and deep …

absaetze.t: Carla Babb is joining Military Times and Defense News as our new Head of Content. In nearly two decades covering national security and international affairs, Babb has earned a reputation for fearless, fact-driven journalism and deep relationships across the U.S. defense establishment.

Recognized as one of the nation’s most candid and well-sourced defense journalists, Babb has broken major stories, pressed senior military leaders for answers and reported from conflict zones around the world. In her new role, she will spearhead editorial initiatives, lead enterprise projects and expand the publications’ presence at major events while developing new ways to engage military, defense industry and national security audiences.

Babb will work alongside Editor-in-Chief J.D. Simkins, who continues to lead coverage by the Military Times and Defense News newsroom. Under Simkins, the newsroom has published its 10 most-read stories of all time within the last year. Simkins was also a recent recipient of the Timothy White Award for Editorial Integrity at SIIA’s Jesse H. Neal Awards. Together, they will lead the next chapter for the brands.

Babb most recently served as national security correspondent for Newsmax and spent more than a decade as Voice of America’s Pentagon correspondent, reaching a global audience of hundreds of millions. She has also reported for Military Times and Defense News.

Babb’s scoops include the 2020 Iranian missile attack on U.S. troops at Iraq’s Al-Asad Air Base, U.S. military interdictions of illicit oil tankers in 2025, and troop deployments and military operations during the 2026 war with Iran. Her interviews with senior military leaders have generated headlines across major national outlets, including The Washington Post, Newsweek, Fox News and NBC News.

“Military Times and Defense News are where service members and their families turn for unvarnished insight and accountability on the issues that shape their lives, and I’m excited about where we can take them next,” said Babb. “I’m eager to get to work with Jon and this newsroom to chase the stories our readers need, widen our coverage and shape national security conversations.”
A prominent advocate for independent defense journalism, Babb serves as vice president of the board of Military Reporters and Editors.

Later this week, Babb will receive the prestigious Prize of Excellence from the Association of Foreign Correspondents in the United States for her outstanding contributions to journalism and distinguished national security reporting. Her work has also earned recognition from the Gerald R. Ford Presidential Foundation, the Press Club of Atlantic City, and regional Associated Press and Society of Professional Journalists chapters.

items.titel: An archaeological take on ancient rituals in the heart of a legendary Berlin nightclub
items.anriss: The artists Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech leveraged AI to bring a 4,000-year old ritual into Berghain

absaetze.t: “The world is changed. I feel it in the water. I feel it in the earth. I smell it in the air. Much that once was is lost, for none now live who remember it.” Cate Blanchett, as the high elf Galadriel, spoke these opening lines in The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), and in darkened cinemas around the world, her delivery set the tone for the wonder that followed. Not since my first viewing of that film 25 years ago had I felt that sense of being dwarfed by mythology, and to re-experience it in Berlin’s famous nightclub Berghain of all places was a delight.

Ala Roushan and Charles Stankievech, an artist duo hailing from Iran and Canada, respectively, expertly blended archaeology, artificial intelligence (AI), acoustics, chemistry and sculpture to create a profoundly multi-sensory experience in A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads earlier this autumn (2-18 October).

Situated inside Halle am Berghain—a gargantuan former power station that, yes, was reminiscent of J.R.R. Tolkien’s Khazad-dûm—the installation was presented by the Berlin-based contemporary art initiative House, helmed by Juliet Kothe, who co-curated with Nadim Samman. The exhibition was co-presented by the Autotelic Foundation, whose whimsical take on AI art in Venice had been one of the standout digital presentations during the most recent Biennale.

At the centre of A Shroud of Woven Solar Threads was a towering, eight-minute-long, 4K video installation that slowly panned through a digitally rendered, 4,000-year-old Mithraic cave temple, created based on 3D scans of the ancient site. Originally made for an exhibition in Lausanne in 2025, the installation was expanded to take advantage of the Halle am Berghain’s size.

As the “camera” floated through the ancient temple in the looping video, visitors were encouraged to position themselves in the center of the installation, where they would be encircled by human-height black monolithic speakers. Each speaker featured a different voice, all chanting in an AI-generated, speculative Proto-Indo-Iranian (PII). PII is the ancestor of the Indo-Aryan and Iranian language families, including Sanskrit and Avestan. There are no historic documents or written texts in PII, let alone documented Mithraic chants from that period.

To realise the vital sonic component of the installation, the artists worked with the University of Toronto, drawing on comparative linguistics to reconstruct plausible linguistic forms. AI then allowed them to bring the speculative language to life. One of the speakers, Roushan said, was based on her own mother’s voice, which had been used to train one of the AI chanters.

"Mithra…" the chant began, referring to the ancient solar deity, a kind of lesser-known Ra, and as the incense burning in the hall filled one’s nostrils it was difficult not to feel transported by the sheer scale and the acoustic prowess of the installation. Near the ceiling, graffiti of the Eye of Horus that pre-dated the exhibition oddly contributed to the compounding of ritualistic symbols that have accumulated in the hall.

There is an inherent futility in worshipping an ancient sun god for any kind of wish-fulfillment. But ritualistic production and devotion have persisted through millennia and in our lives today, be it in our fascination with our illuminated, hand-held screens, or our commitment to attend public dance events that encourage abandon—such as the one that took place the weekend of Roushan and Stankievech’s opening, several metres and a few layers of concrete away. Objects scattered throughout the exhibition space included replicas of Bronze Age bells and reliefs, objects of ritual and religious significance that adorned the space and further contextualised the spiritual dimension of the installation, although none so potent as the ever-burning incense.

“We are all subject to digital change in society, economy, politics,” Nadim Samman, the Autotelic Foundation’s director, says. “These changes are massive, they are abrupt and they are intense. Making sense of it needs to come from below. Artists offer important ways to understand what this change means. Without artists, we are just stuck with the narratives and the images supplied by the companies that make the technology. Digital change impacts culture, and artists can help us understand what that impact actually feels like, and how we can think it through."

Since we have no recordings of PII, it is hard to refute that AI contributed a vital component of the installation. The exhibition’s thoughtful and archaeological approach to incorporating technologies that help us to speculate on the past was a welcome counterpoint to many digital art exhibitions in recent memory.

Roushan and Stankievech’s ambitious undertaking stands as one of the highlights of what has been a busy year for digital and AI-generated artistic presentations. The rather romantic gesture of leveraging AI to take us back several thousand years, to a time of fascination with nature and solar worship, and the decision to do so within the Brutalist context of a power-station-cum-nightclub, cleverly brought together many disparate threads.

items.titel: Comment | A missed opportunity for a full accounting of cultural cleansing
items.anriss: A Paris exhibition on heritage destruction fails to confront cultural genocide in Gaza and exposes the double standards of international institutions

absaetze.t: It is always gratifying to see one’s work referenced—especially 20 years after the fact. The exhibition Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, at the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine in Paris (until 3 January 2027), traces attacks on material and intangible culture in conflicts beginning with the dynamiting of the Bamiyan Buddhas in 2001 and ending in Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza.
The vast exhibition spans art, digital re-creations, photography and filmed interviews. It is conceived of as an investigative report organised into sections on erasure, resistance and repair.

A wall text references my 2006 book The Destruction of Memory: Architecture at War, which first set out systematically why such targeting happens. The exhibition credits me with coining the term “cultural cleansing” in respect of the Bosnian War to explain the pattern of heritage erasure that can accompany, or presage, ethnic cleansing and the persecution of populations. It notes that Unesco adopted the term from 2012 to describe “the destruction of World Heritage Sites by terrorist groups”.

Except that book says much more than that. It talked about this same process in other places such as the Israel-occupied West Bank. It examined cultural genocide (like cultural cleansing, this still has no definition in international law) witnessed in instances ranging from the Ottoman Empire and Native American populations to the Holocaust and Tibet. I would now add the experiences of the Uyghurs in China, the Rohingya in Myanmar, the Yazidis in Iraq and the Palestinians in Gaza to that dreadful list. I argue that patterns of heritage destruction can evidence genocidal intent. Other genocides, such as that in Rwanda, did not have a pronounced material culture component.

These are matters that the Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine exhibition unacceptably skirts. As in Germany and the UK (where a talk at London’s Building Centre including Architects for Gaza was cancelled following an intervention by Lawyers for Israel this summer), the French state and its institutions are censoring pro-Palestinian voices.The crucial work of Forensic Architecture in documenting destruction, for example, is not present after a dispute over the group’s use of “the G word”. How can you explain what has happened to Gaza’s cultural heritage unless you are at least prepared to discuss possible intent and patterns of destruction?

As an investigative report, the show obfuscates as much as it reveals. Institutions and governments shield themselves behind the argument that it is up to the courts to determine genocide. They forget the Genocide Convention’s duties of prevention—as litigated in the 2007 International Court of Justice (ICJ) case, Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro, or South Africa’s inclusion of attacks on culture when considering Palestinian “conditions of life” at the ICJ.

There is an impression that heritage destruction in conflicts has got worse over recent decades and that the propaganda impact of destruction is actually exploited by some groups. The jury is out on this. As reflected in the show, however, the international heritage community has had an almost singular focus on actions by terrorist groups, whereas over the past decades (Islamic State and its affiliates aside) it has been the firepower of United Nations State Parties that has been overwhelmingly responsible for the devastation to material history—including but not limited to the United States, Russia, China, Israel and Saudi Arabia. Isis iconoclastically wrecked religious sites in Mosul, but it was the liberating forces that comprehensively flattened the historic city.
Does loot support terrorism?

Looting, too, is problematically covered in the Paris exhibition. This is a serious issue in war zones where security vanishes. But the myth repeated here that the sale of looted artefacts is a meaningful source of terrorist funding “on a par” with resources such as oil is simply unevidenced. (Recovered Isis documents show something quite different.)

The exhibition is sponsored in part by the French office of Unesco. No surprise then that the organisation’s manifest failure to protect heritage in conflicts is absent from the walls. Unesco is celebrated—as it should be in some cases—for its work in Timbuktu, where the International Criminal Court brought the first (and, to date, only) successful prosecution for the targeting of monuments as a war crime. Less convincingly, the show argues that this episode was a turning point after which Unesco formulated a more grassroots approach to preserving culture by working with local people on local priorities.

It was Unesco that disgracefully praised Putin for liberating Palmyra despite the terrible damage Russian forces allied with Assad inflicted on Syria’s people and heritage. Unesco has been just as partial since: while it “strongly condemns” Russian attacks on heritage in Ukraine and Israel’s on Lebanon, it does not offer the same degree of pressure in its statements on heritage destruction in Gaza or Iran. Even then, unlike other UN agencies, Unesco never names Israel. Unesco has not invoked the 1954 Hague Convention in relation to Gaza, despite citing it in virtually all similar instances. Unesco did not seek urgent action by the UN Security Council or the General Assembly to protect cultural sites there as it did in respect of Isis.

The Paris show is more subtle in its understanding of the ways that post-war heritage reconstruction can be problematic and not necessarily healing, but is just as silent on Unesco’s move away from the centrality of authenticity to reconstruction work. Whereas the notion of rebuilding the Bamiyan Buddhas was deemed unacceptable, Unesco promoted building a brand-new Mostar Bridge in Bosnia and Herzegovina as peacebuilding—despite community relations actually deteriorating in the city. And then the agency had the temerity to declare the facsimile bridge a World Heritage Site, undermining its own scientific tenets to bolster a failed symbolic gesture. All this bad-faith is set out in my follow-up book, Monumental Lies (2022).

One is left to read between the lines for hints at the full curatorial mindset. Once through the exhibition doors, the first large-scale works displayed are photographs by the Palestinian artist Taysir Batniji of Gazans’ retrieved housekeys, with their heartbreakingly quotidian fobs—a friendship bracelet, a cheap carabiner clip, a Minnie Mouse figure. The unknown fate of their owners is pencilled in below.

In its silences and voids, Heritage in Resistance at least accurately mirrors failures of international institutions and laws and the partiality and misinformation that surrounds responses to contemporary heritage destruction. Ultimately, the show offers false hope about successful resistance via digital surveying, reconstruction and Unesco work. What we should be feeling is despair.
Heritage in Resistance: Timbuktu to Odessa, until 3 January 2027, Cité de l’Architecture et du Patrimoine, Paris
Robert Bevan is a journalist, author and heritage consultant

items.titel: Weimer schlägt Bremen als Gedenkort für Kolonialismus vor
items.anriss: Weimer schlägt Bremen als Gedenkort für Kolonialismus vor Daniel Völzke Wed, 11/25/2026 - 22:39

absaetze.t: Arbeitspapier
Vor einem Jahr versprach der Kulturstaatsminister ein eigenes Konzept zur Erinnerung an das Unrecht des Kolonialismus. Jetzt hat er ein Arbeitspapier vorgelegt

Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer will in Bremen einen Ort der Erinnerung an das Unrecht und die Opfer des deutschen Kolonialismus schaffen. Der Vorschlag steht in einem 17-seitigen Papier des Bundesbeauftragten für Kultur und Medien zur "Aufarbeitung des Kolonialismus", das der Deutschen Presse-Agentur vorliegt. Auch die "Zeit" berichtete darüber.

Den Vorschlag Bremen begründet Weimer damit, dass die Stadt eine besondere kolonialhistorische Bedeutung habe. Dort gebe es seit langem zivilgesellschaftliches Engagement und auch Forschung zum Thema. Auch dem Übersee-Museum komme eine besondere Rolle zu.

Zunächst soll aber eine Machbarkeitsstudie prüfen, unter welchen Voraussetzungen die Institution in der Hansestadt entstehen könnte. Dazu sollen auch Vertreter aus ehemals kolonialisierten Gebieten gehört werden. Im Falle einer positiven Entscheidung soll das Übersee-Museum die Federführung bekommen.
Kolonialpolitik "menschenverachtend"

"Das Deutsche Kaiserreich verfolgte eine rücksichtslose koloniale Expansionspolitik", heißt es in dem Arbeitspapier. Es erinnert an die deutschen kolonialen Interessen in Afrika, Ozeanien und China, an Gewalt, Sklavenhandel und Machtpolitik. Allein auf dem Gebiet des heutigen Namibia wurden schätzungsweise 100.000 Angehörige der Herero und Nama getötet. Das Papier betont: "Die Mittel, mit denen das deutsche Kaiserreich seine Kolonialpolitik umsetzte, waren menschenverachtend."

Weimer bezeichnet die Rückgabe menschlicher Überreste und Kulturgüter aus "kolonialen Kontexten" als ethische und politische Verpflichtung. Einer Bestandsaufnahme zufolge befänden sich mindestens 17.000 menschliche Überreste in 33 öffentlichen deutschen Einrichtungen. Wichtig sind jedoch aus Weimers Sicht detaillierte Informationen.
Provenienzforschung soll gestärkt werden

Er betont die Bedeutung von Provenienzforschung. Dafür sollen auch Institutionen wie die Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz, das Humboldt Forum, die Kulturstiftung des Bundes, das Deutsche Zentrum Kulturgutverluste, das Deutsche Historische Museum und das Bundesarchiv gestärkt werden. Ein internationales Wissenschaftsnetz soll Experten aus den ehemals kolonialisierten Gebieten einbeziehen.

Weimer hatte vor einem Jahr ein neues Gedenkstättenkonzept vorgelegt, das Thema Kolonialismus aber bewusst außen vor gelassen. Dafür erntete er Kritik von Forschern und Verbänden. Weimers Vorgängerin Claudia Roth (Grüne) wollte das Thema in die Gedenkstättenkonzeption aufnehmen, doch wurde ihr Konzept zu Zeiten der Ampel-Koalition nicht mehr beschlossen.

items.titel: Adobe's Creative Agent transforms Creative Cloud tools and Firefly workflows
items.anriss: Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives "more time for their craft".

absaetze.t: Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives “more time for their craft”.
Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the update spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.
Photoshop now features generative restyle and relight, Premiere has a new colour mode, and InDesign now supports co-editing (beta).
Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to Firefly – its AI creative studio – through the Firefly AI Assistant, which is currently in beta.
Users can direct the assistant in plain language, with Adobe stating it has already been used for everything from batch retouching portraits to turning product shots into short-form social videos.
The aim is to help creators take on projects that may previously have required more time, resources or technical complexity.
Adobe has also launched Firefly Design in beta, a single workspace that combines raster and vector graphics with motion, 3D and print design.
Available as part of Creative Cloud, Firefly Design allows designers to build, review, and hand over projects without leaving the platform.
Topaz Labs, now part of Adobe, has released two new image-enhancement models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, which are sold separately through Topaz.
Adobe said the Creative Cloud updates respond to the way creatives are increasingly working – juggling more formats, apps and mediums while being asked to turn projects around faster.
The brand’s latest approach aims to tackle this by bringing “AI assistance and collaboration directly into the Adobe tools they rely on”.
Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud at Adobe, said the aim is to protect what makes a creative’s work distinctive.
“The ideas, taste, style and vision that creative professionals bring to their work are what make their work stand out,” said Subramaniam.

“Our latest Creative Cloud innovations transform our trusted creative tools into agentic, intelligent workflows that give pros the precision, control and flexibility to explore their ideas, streamline their work and stay focused on the creative decisions that make their work uniquely theirs.”

The Creative Agent – which Adobe describes as a creative partner – now powers AI Assistants (currently in beta) across Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects and Frame.io. In Photoshop, the assistant is available only in the Photoshop beta app.
The agent handles multi-step tasks behind the scenes, letting professionals delegate work and increase their creative velocity while remaining “in the director’s chair”.

In Premiere, the agent now supports new capabilities, including applying an effect to every clip in a sequence, tracking a masked subject through a frame, and adjusting colour and exposure across a whole sequence at once.
Adobe is also previewing local MCP integrations, which allow external AI agents to connect with its software.
The integrations will let users instruct third-party agents of their choice to work inside Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects, editing project files directly on their own computer.

Layers, vectors and sequences stay fully editable throughout the process, so users can “step in at any moment to refine the work by hand”. The local MCP integrations will be available in private beta in early 2027.

If a user’s chosen third-party agent is also connected to other MCP-capable tools, such as Google Drive or Slack, it can bring them into the same workflow. For example, it could pull in a brief from Google Docs, work on the project using Adobe’s tools and share the result with colleagues in Slack.

Adobe has also added several updates that give Firefly users more say over how the AI assistant works. Creatives are now able to save their preferred formats, colours, brand guidelines, characters and products to be applied consistently in future projects.

A new plan mode lets users review, edit and approve the agent’s plan before it starts, or leave the agent to run on its own. Adobe explained that creators remain in control, “guiding the work and making creative decisions as their projects evolve”.
Users can also choose which AI model the agent works with, or let the agent select the best fit for the task.
In Firefly Boards, the agent can help develop mood boards, storyboards and concepts through conversation as they take shape in real time, “guided by human taste and direction”.
Adobe also introduced a preview of always-on agents to carry out routine jobs, such as sorting new files or preparing content for different platforms, “even when the customer steps away”.
Firefly’s video, design and image editors have also been updated, with the aim of taking projects from initial idea to finished work in a single workflow.
Among the other additions are a gallery of ready-made, quick actions, visual boards, and node-bases workflows through Firefly Graph (beta), which lets users build repeatable workflows of their own.
Adobe’s examples include turning a video storyboard into a finished cut and, in Firefly Design, carrying a brand identity from initial concept through client review within a single design workspace.
To learn more about the updates, visit Adobe’s website.
